stemMd: Two independent surveys were conducted, each using a random sample of residents, to estimate the percentage of residents who support building a new bike lane. In Town P, $48\%$ of the sample supported it, with an associated margin of error of $3$ percentage points. In Town Q, $52\%$ of the sample supported it, with an associated margin of error of $4$ percentage points. Which statement is best supported by these results?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The percentage of all Town Q residents who support the bike lane is greater than the percentage of all Town P residents who support it.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It is plausible that the percentage of all Town P residents who support the bike lane is greater than the percentage of all Town Q residents who support it.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Fewer than half of all Town P residents support the bike lane.

options.label: D
options.textMd: More than half of all Town Q residents support the bike lane.

explanationMd:
Turn each estimate into the range of plausible values for the whole town before comparing anything.

$$\text{Town P: } 48\% \pm 3 \;\Rightarrow\; 45\% \text{ to } 51\%$$

$$\text{Town Q: } 52\% \pm 4 \;\Rightarrow\; 48\% \text{ to } 56\%$$

A statement about the towns is supported only if it holds for **every** plausible value, and a statement that something is *plausible* is supported if it holds for **some** pair of plausible values.

- The two ranges overlap from $48\%$ to $51\%$. Town P could plausibly be at $50\%$ while Town Q is at $49\%$, so it is plausible that Town P's percentage is the greater one. That is the supported statement.
- Because of that same overlap, the data do not establish that Town Q's percentage is greater than Town P's, even though Town Q's sample percentage is higher.
- Town Q's range includes values below $50\%$, so it is not established that more than half of Town Q supports the lane.
- Town P's range includes values above $50\%$ (up to $51\%$), so it is not established that fewer than half of Town P supports it.

The lesson: when two margin-of-error ranges overlap, the samples do not show which population percentage is larger.

distractorRationale.a: This compares only the sample percentages. The plausible ranges, $45\%$ to $51\%$ for Town P and $48\%$ to $56\%$ for Town Q, overlap, so the data do not show which town's true percentage is higher.
distractorRationale.d: Town Q's plausible range is $48\%$ to $56\%$, which includes values below $50\%$, so the results do not establish that more than half of Town Q supports the lane.
distractorRationale.c: Town P's plausible range is $45\%$ to $51\%$, which includes values above $50\%$, so the results do not establish that fewer than half of Town P supports the lane.

accessibilityText: Random-sample surveys in two towns estimated support for a new bike lane. Town P: 48 percent, margin of error 3 percentage points. Town Q: 52 percent, margin of error 4 percentage points. Which statement is best supported? The choices are: the percentage of all Town Q residents who support the lane is greater than the percentage for Town P; it is plausible that the percentage of all Town P residents who support the lane is greater than the percentage for Town Q; fewer than half of all Town P residents support the lane; more than half of all Town Q residents support the lane.

provenance.notes: Original item. Two margin-of-error intervals that overlap and that each straddle 50 percent, so only the 'plausible' comparison survives; tests reading intervals rather than point estimates.

independentSolve.workingNotes: P interval 45-51%, Q interval 48-56%; they overlap, so P > Q is plausible. A asserts a difference not established; C fails because P's interval reaches 51%; D fails because Q's interval goes down to 48%. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-math-run1) reached the same answer: Intervals: P 45-51%, Q 48-56%; they overlap, so P > Q is plausible. A is not established (overlap); C and D fail because both intervals contain 50%.]
